notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Orange double reflectors on the front and a single white one on the back; rarer blue and red versions. Only Czechia has the same design.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: A new standard wedge bollard with a red front reflector, like Hungary's, is being introduced but is still very rare.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: A special wide B-type guardrail used nowhere else in Europe but Czechia; here other types appear occasionally too.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Wide round concrete poles, often paired, with short metal bars holding the insulators.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Pole tops sometimes show two support bars forming an upside-down triangle; trident-style tops with two upward arms are unique to this country and Czechia.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Striped gas and water marker poles that resemble snow poles stand beside roads, though stripy utility poles exist across Europe.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are white with red arrows; less commonly red on yellow.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Hiking markers with one coloured stripe between two white ones, sometimes forming an arrow, are very common; some appear in Poland, Hungary and Germany.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue direction signs with small white arrows; Czechia has large filled white arrows.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: The painted border on signs sits right at the edge; Czech signs leave a strip of background colour outside it. Motorway signs can be blue or green.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road signs use a very bold font; Czech signs have a much thinner one.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Street signs are white with blue text and a thin red border, with "ulica" in the name. House numbers are on white signs with a thin red or black border.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Two five-stripe pedestrian signs: a simple belted figure, or one with the stripes squeezed close together.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Kilometre markers have two sections split by a black horizontal line, with the road number on top.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Cycling route signs use the letter C as their symbol, unique to this country, in a style like the hiking markers.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Railway crossing signs have a white rectangular background; Czech ones have none.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Sign posts are open or topped with a grey metal cap or thin black cap; most Czech ones have a thick black cap.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Slavic language with acute accents plus Ľ, Ô, Ä, Ŕ and Ĺ. Czech instead has Ř, Ě and Ů.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Prefab panel apartment blocks, well maintained and painted in bright colours and patterns, like Czechia.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Shutters are far more common than in Czechia, and many houses face the road with their short side and a hip roof end, as in Hungary.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Diamond-shaped roof tiles are common; grey metal roofs are very common, especially in the east.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Ranges from very mountainous to completely flat; Czechia is generally hillier but less mountainous.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Much Generation 3 coverage has an antenna with grey tape on top, also seen in Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. Spring coverage is plentiful here.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Roads numbered 500 to 560 and the 4-digit ones generally increase from west to east.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Completely flat farmland stretching past the horizon in the western lowlands, rare elsewhere in the country.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Wide flat fields ringed by distant hills or mountains in the eastern lowlands.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Several southern areas have a Hungarian majority, with bilingual street and information signs.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Concrete poles in the Nitra and Trnava regions often have painted yellow circles, usually holding a number.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Yellow lamp posts with a blue base are mainly in the east, except around Zvolen.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Pine forests are common in the westernmost part.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Bilingual town entry signs in Rusyn, a Cyrillic language close to Ukrainian, in the northeast of Prešov region.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Only two cities have trams: a red one in the capital and a yellow-blue-white one in Košice.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Red street signs in the northwest corner town of Skalica, like Czechia's but in a stylised font.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Dark brown wooden houses with white line art on the walls mark a village in the westernmost Žilina region.
